evidence.title: Empirical data drift detection experiments on real-world medical imaging data
evidence.outcome: Timeliness of drift detection given sample size requirements for alerting
evidence.effect: Detection needs about 4000 new CXRs, which may take days at large providers or months at smaller ones, so alerts may not be timely enough for clinicians to intervene.
evidence.quote: This finding has direct implications for the practical use of drift detection techniques: if it takes days (large radiology providers) or months (smaller providers) to perform 4000 new CXRs, then existing techniques for drift detection may not be timely enough to allow clinicians using the tool to intervene promptly.

commentary.bottom_line: Eleven studies suggest that predefined statistical thresholds can flag model degradation and prompt retraining, but all are descriptive deployments, simulations, or benchmarks, and none measured patient outcomes. One prospective comparison found that drift alerts missed the months when performance fell, so drift thresholds alone may not be enough.

perspectives.view: Four real-deployment studies are level 3 descriptive reports, and the other seven are simulations or automated benchmarks. Outcomes are detection or model accuracy rather than patient harm, which makes the evidence indirect. One prospective comparison returned mixed results. Certainty that the practice prevents late or ignored degradation is very low.

In one deployment, an AUC of 0.73 fell below a 0.85 threshold and triggered fine-tuning that restored AUC to 0.873. In a Dutch cohort, AUC fell below the ±3 SD limit in March 2020 and March 2021, yet drift detection flagged neither month. This suggests performance thresholds may catch failures that drift thresholds miss.

Control-chart methods flagged 3.0% of regions as outliers and identified a humerus performance drop that end users also recognized. A 2σ limit caught milder deviations than a 3σ limit. CUSUM sensitivity can be tuned to trade false alarms against detection delay, with almost no false alarms in 60 days at 40 samples per day.

Detecting drift in chest radiographs required about 4000 new images, which may take days at large providers and months at smaller ones. In simulations, shift-triggered updating outperformed fixed-interval updating, and a risk-score trigger detected drift about six weeks before complaint-driven surveillance would have. Smaller systems may need longer windows or pooled data.

FDA draft guidance and discussion papers expect sponsors to specify drift analyses and thresholds. One study showed a threshold written into a predetermined change control plan triggering retraining at one site and no action at another where AUC stayed above threshold. This suggests the plan mechanism can operate as designed in a single case.

One benchmark used 130486 retinal images with a racial and ethnic minority focus and kept Type I error near the chosen 5% level while detecting many shifts. No study tested subgroup equity thresholds in a live deployment. One hazard study found the false positive rate for a quality metric rose from 81.6% to 85.7% as covariates shifted.

commentary.research_gap: No study compared threshold-based alerting with usual monitoring on patient harm, time to corrective action, or staff response. It also remains unknown how often alerts were acted on, how subgroup equity thresholds perform in practice, and how low-volume sites can reach the sample sizes needed for timely detection.
commentary.underserved_note: No test of the practice enrolled Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations; one offline benchmark had a racial and ethnic minority focus. Because detection may take months at lower-volume sites, safety-net systems may face longer delays before thresholds fire, and the current evidence does not show whether the practice works for them.
